This is not a caricature; it is the observable, documented incentive structure of public institutions. As economist Murray Rothbard argued, government monopoly over protective services is no more justified than monopoly over food production—and the consequences of the former are arguably worse, because they involve the mechanisms of force itself.

The philosopher Robert Nozick demonstrated in Anarchy, State, and Utopia that even the minimal state requires justification, and that the burden of proof rests on those who would concentrate power rather than distribute it. The Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises showed that without genuine price signals—which only emerge in competitive markets—rational resource allocation is impossible. If centralized provision of shoes or bread leads to shortages and poor quality (as it invariably has in command economies), why would centralized provision of security and justice be any different?

The answer, consistently, is that it is not different. Government-run essential services suffer from the same calculation problems, the same bureaucratic ossification, and the same accountability failures that plague every monopoly enterprise in history.

II. The Economic Case: Competition Breeds Excellence

A. Private Security Is Already Superior

The evidence for private security's superiority is not speculative—it is already manifest in the existing economy. In the United States alone, private security personnel outnumber public police officers by roughly three to one. Corporations, residential communities, universities, shopping centers, hospitals, and millions of individuals already trust their safety to private firms rather than relying exclusively on public police.

Why? Because private security providers are contractually obligated to deliver specific outcomes. They can be fired. Their contracts can be renegotiated. They must compete for clients. This competitive pressure produces measurable results: faster response times, more personalized service, greater attentiveness to client needs, and a focus on prevention rather than after-the-fact reaction.

Consider gated communities with private security: they consistently report lower crime rates than comparable neighborhoods relying solely on municipal police. Private security firms working for retailers have dramatically reduced shoplifting losses through sophisticated analytics and proactive strategies that public police departments lack the resources or incentive to develop.

The Detroit Threat Management Center, a private security firm operating in one of America's most dangerous cities, has protected its clients for decades with zero homicides in their coverage areas—a record no municipal police department in a comparable environment can approach. This is not an anomaly; it is the predictable result of an organization whose survival depends on actually protecting people.

B. Private Arbitration Already Outperforms Public Courts

The superiority of private arbitration over state courts is even more decisively demonstrated. The American legal system is, by nearly universal acknowledgment, a slow, expensive, and frequently unjust mechanism for resolving disputes. Civil cases routinely take years to resolve. Criminal cases are overwhelmingly settled through plea bargaining—a process that has little to do with justice and everything to do with managing an overwhelmed system. The backlog in many jurisdictions numbers in the hundreds of thousands.

Meanwhile, private arbitration—already the preferred dispute resolution mechanism in international commerce, labor relations, securities, construction, and technology—resolves disputes in weeks or months rather than years. It costs a fraction of litigation. It allows parties to select arbitrators with genuine expertise in the relevant subject matter, rather than relying on generalist judges who may know nothing about the technical issues at hand.

The effectiveness of private arbitration is so well established that the vast majority of commercial contracts now include mandatory arbitration clauses. Businesses with billions of dollars at stake voluntarily choose private adjudication over public courts. This is perhaps the most powerful endorsement possible: when people are free to choose, they consistently choose private justice.

Organizations like the American Arbitration Association, JAMS, and the International Chamber of Commerce's International Court of Arbitration process hundreds of thousands of cases annually with satisfaction rates that dwarf those of public court users. The lex mercatoria—the body of commercial law developed entirely through private merchant courts during the medieval period—demonstrates that private legal systems are not merely theoretically possible but historically proven over centuries.

C. Cost Efficiency and Innovation

Government services are structurally incapable of achieving the cost efficiency that competitive markets produce. Public police departments operate under collective bargaining agreements that make it nearly impossible to dismiss underperforming officers. Procurement processes are governed by political considerations rather than value optimization. Budgets are determined by political negotiation rather than performance metrics.

Private firms, by contrast, face constant pressure to reduce costs and improve quality. They adopt new technologies faster, restructure operations more readily, and allocate resources based on demonstrated need rather than political lobbying. The explosion of innovation in private security—from advanced surveillance analytics and AI-driven threat assessment to cybersecurity services and sophisticated access control systems—has been driven entirely by market competition. Public police departments, meanwhile, frequently operate with outdated technology, antiquated information systems, and training programs that have remained functionally unchanged for decades.

Economist Edward Stringham's research in Private Governance documents dozens of cases in which private institutions have created order and resolved disputes more effectively than state systems. From the London Stock Exchange's self-regulatory mechanisms to eBay's private dispute resolution system (which handles sixty million disputes annually—more than the entire American civil court system), private governance is not a libertarian fantasy; it is the dominant reality in an enormous portion of human interaction.

III. The Accountability Argument: Market Discipline vs. Democratic Illusion

Perhaps the most common objection to privatizing police and courts is that "democratic accountability" provides a check on government power that private firms lack. This argument collapses under scrutiny.

Democratic accountability for essential services is, in practice, almost entirely illusory. Citizens vote for elected officials once every two to four years, rarely on the basis of specific policies regarding police operations or court administration. The actual bureaucrats who run these institutions are unelected, protected by civil service rules, and functionally immune to public pressure. Police officers who commit misconduct are protected by qualified immunity and powerful unions. Judges serve for life or for long terms and are insulated from community needs by design.

Compare this to market accountability. A private security firm that fails to protect its clients loses its contract immediately, not at the next election. A private arbitration service that renders unjust decisions loses its reputation and its client base. The feedback mechanism is direct, continuous, and consequential. You don't need to organize a political campaign, win a majority, and hope that the new administration implements reform. You simply take your business elsewhere.

The philosopher Hans-Hermann Hoppe has argued persuasively that private property-based defense and adjudication systems provide incomparably stronger accountability than democratic governance. In a private system, the provider bears the costs of failure directly. In a government system, the costs of failure are externalized onto taxpayers and victims, while the failing institution continues to operate—and often expands.

Consider the American criminal justice system's track record: the Innocence Project has documented hundreds of wrongful convictions, many involving decades of imprisonment. Government prosecutors who secured these convictions faced no meaningful consequences. Government-employed forensic labs have been exposed fabricating evidence in multiple jurisdictions. Police departments have been found operating unconstitutional quota systems, engaging in systematic civil rights violations, and maintaining "blue walls of silence" that shield criminal behavior within their ranks.

These are not aberrations; they are the predictable consequences of monopoly power exercised without genuine accountability. No private firm could survive such a record. Only governments can fail catastrophically and continue to demand payment from their victims.

IV. Historical and Contemporary Evidence

A. Historical Private Law Systems

The claim that private justice systems are untested or utopian is historically illiterate. Some of the most celebrated legal traditions in Western civilization were privately generated:

  • Medieval Iceland's Commonwealth (930–1262 AD) operated for over three centuries with no executive branch, no police force, and a legal system based entirely on private enforcement and competitive chieftaincies (goðorð). Disputes were resolved through a sophisticated system in which individuals chose their own legal representatives and enforcement was privatized. The system produced one of the most literate, legally sophisticated, and relatively peaceful societies of its era, as documented by scholars David Friedman and Jesse Byock.

  • The Law Merchant (Lex Mercatoria) governed international trade for centuries through entirely private courts and enforcement mechanisms. Merchants voluntarily submitted to private adjudication and accepted the reputational consequences of noncompliance. This system was so effective that its principles were eventually absorbed into public commercial law—not because the private system failed, but because it succeeded.

  • The Kapauku Papuans of West New Guinea, studied by anthropologist Leopold Pospíšil, maintained a complex legal system with private adjudication and no state enforcement. Property rights were strong, disputes were resolved efficiently, and the system persisted for generations.

  • Celtic Ireland operated for roughly a thousand years under the Brehon law system, which featured competing private courts, professional jurists who derived their authority from reputation rather than state appointment, and enforcement based on surety and social pressure rather than state coercion.

These are not cherry-picked examples; they represent a broad pattern. As legal scholar Bruce Benson documents in The Enterprise of Law, private legal systems have emerged spontaneously across cultures, centuries, and continents. State monopolization of law is the historical exception, not the rule.

B. Contemporary Private Governance

In the modern world, private governance already handles an enormous and growing share of dispute resolution, security, and rule enforcement:

  • Online platforms like eBay, Amazon, and Alibaba govern hundreds of millions of transactions through private rules, private dispute resolution, and reputational enforcement mechanisms. These systems are faster, cheaper, and more accessible than any court system on earth.

  • Homeowners associations govern approximately 74 million Americans—roughly one in four—through private contractual rule systems with private enforcement.

  • Private communities in countries with weak state institutions, from South Africa to Brazil, have developed sophisticated private security and governance structures that demonstrably outperform the public services available to them.

  • International commercial arbitration governs trillions of dollars in global commerce, with enforcement rates that exceed those of many national court judgments, thanks to the New York Convention and the reputational incentives facing arbitral institutions.

V. Addressing Objections

A. "The Poor Would Be Unprotected"

This is the most emotionally powerful objection, and the most misleading. Under the current system, the poor are unprotected. Public police departments demonstrably underserve low-income communities. Response times in poor neighborhoods are dramatically longer. Clearance rates for crimes against poor victims are far lower. The criminal justice system disproportionately incarcerates the poor while failing to protect them.

In a competitive private system, entrepreneurs would have powerful incentives to develop low-cost security solutions for underserved markets—just as they have in telecommunications, banking, and retail. The mobile phone revolution brought communication to billions of poor people whom government telephone monopolies had failed for decades. There is no reason to expect security to be different. Insurance-based models, community cooperatives, mutual aid societies, and philanthropic funding would all emerge to serve populations currently abandoned by government services.

Moreover, the enormous savings from eliminating government bureaucratic waste could fund charitable security provision for the truly indigent. The American criminal justice system costs taxpayers over $300 billion annually. Even a fraction of those savings, redirected through competitive markets and voluntary charity, would provide dramatically better protection for the poor than they currently receive.

B. "Private Police Would Become Warlords"

This objection confuses privatization with lawlessness. A fully privatized system does not mean the abolition of rules; it means competitive, market-based provision of rule enforcement. Private security firms would operate under contractual obligations, insurance requirements, and reputational constraints far more binding than the weak oversight currently governing public police.

Insurance companies—which would underwrite private security operations—have powerful financial incentives to ensure that their clients behave lawfully and ethically. A private security firm that used excessive force would face immediate contractual liability, loss of insurance, loss of clients, and potential criminal prosecution (under whatever meta-legal framework governs the system). Compare this to public police officers, who routinely escape consequences for far worse behavior under qualified immunity and the protection of their unions and departments.

The "warlord" scenario is further undermined by the economic logic of violence. Violence is expensive. Cooperation is profitable. Private firms seeking to maximize long-term revenue have every incentive to resolve disputes peacefully and maintain reputations for fairness. The entities that most closely resemble warlords in modern society are not private businesses; they are governments—organizations that claim monopoly authority over defined territories and fund themselves through compulsory extraction (taxation).

C. "Some Services Are Natural Monopolies"

The natural monopoly argument has been systematically debunked by economists across the spectrum. Virtually every service once claimed to be a natural monopoly—telephone, electricity, water, mail delivery—has been successfully subjected to competition in at least some jurisdictions, with the predicted benefits of lower costs and improved quality materializing consistently. The historical evidence shows that the "natural monopoly" designation has almost always been a post-hoc justification for politically-motivated monopolization, not a genuine economic phenomenon.

Even in cases where economies of scale are significant, the relevant comparison is not between perfect competition and monopoly, but between regulated monopoly and contestable markets. A market with even the possibility of competitive entry disciplines incumbent providers far more effectively than any regulatory body ever has.

VI. The Moral Imperative

Beyond efficiency and practicality, there is a deeper moral argument for privatization. Government-run essential services are funded through taxation—the compulsory extraction of wealth under threat of imprisonment. Every government service, no matter how beneficial, rests on this foundation of coercion. The privatization of essential services would replace coercion with consent, compulsion with choice, and political power with economic freedom.

The moral philosopher Michael Huemer has argued in The Problem of Political Authority that governments do not possess legitimate authority to monopolize essential services—that no plausible ethical theory grants a group of people the right to forcibly prevent others from competing in the provision of security or justice. If it would be wrong for a private company to force you to buy its services at gunpoint, it is equally wrong for the state to do the same.

The complete privatization of essential services is not merely a policy proposal; it is the logical extension of the principles that underlie every free society: voluntary association, individual rights, and the accountability that only competition provides.

Conclusion

The evidence—philosophical, economic, historical, and empirical—points overwhelmingly in one direction. Government monopolization of essential services produces the same results as every other monopoly: high costs, poor quality, systematic unaccountability, and the abuse of captive consumers. Private security already outperforms public police in the contexts where it operates. Private arbitration already outperforms public courts by virtually every measure. Historical and contemporary examples of private governance demonstrate that voluntary, competitive provision of law and order is neither utopian nor unprecedented—it is a proven model with a track record spanning centuries and continents.

The complete privatization of all essential government services, including police forces and courts, would unleash the same forces of innovation, accountability, and efficiency that have transformed every other sector subjected to genuine competition. The question is not whether markets can provide these services effectively—they already do, and they already have. The question is how much longer we will tolerate the demonstrable failures of monopoly government before we embrace the superior alternative that liberty and competition offer.

The burden of proof has always rested on those who would concentrate power. It is time they acknowledged that they have not met it.

The Case for Private Justice: A Speech

"Free the Law"

Ladies and gentlemen,

I. The Myth of the Monopoly's Necessity

We've been told since childhood that law enforcement and courts must be government monopolies — that without the state's exclusive grip on justice, chaos would reign. But this isn't an argument. It's an assumption. And it's an assumption contradicted by history, by economics, and by the daily reality you experience.

Consider: you lock your doors at night not because of police, but despite the fact that police will likely arrive long after any threat has passed. Many of you already pay for private security systems, gated communities, or personal protection. Exposed communities increasingly hire private patrol services because public police are stretched thin, misallocated, or simply absent.

You are already privatizing your safety. I'm simply asking you to acknowledge it — and to take the principle to its logical, liberating conclusion.

The medieval Icelandic Commonwealth operated for over three centuries with privatized law. The Law Merchant — lex mercatoria — governed international trade for hundreds of years through private arbitration, without a single state court. Today, the majority of commercial disputes worldwide are resolved through private arbitration — not government courts. Visa and Mastercard adjudicate millions of disputes annually with speed and efficiency that would make any Superior Court judge weep.

Private justice is not a utopian fantasy. It is the historical norm that government monopolized and degraded.

II. The Failure of Government Justice

Let me be direct about what the current system delivers.

On policing:

The average response time for a 911 call in a major American city is over ten minutes. In rural areas, it can exceed thirty. The clearance rate for property crime hovers around 14 percent. For burglary, it's closer to 10. That means nine out of ten times someone breaks into your home, no one is held accountable.

Meanwhile, police budgets consume 25 to 40 percent of municipal general funds. Exposed communities — the poor, minorities, rural residents — receive the worst service while bearing disproportionate costs, both financial and in the form of aggressive, unaccountable policing. The system simultaneously over-polices and under-protects.

And accountability? Officers are investigated by their own departments. Prosecutors who depend on police cooperation are asked to hold those same officers to account. Unions negotiate contracts that purge disciplinary records. The structure doesn't merely permit abuse — it architecturally guarantees it.

On courts:

The average federal civil case takes over two years to resolve. Criminal defendants — presumed innocent — wait months or years in jail because they cannot afford bail. Public defenders carry caseloads of hundreds, sometimes over a thousand cases simultaneously. A system that theoretically promises equal justice delivers assembly-line processing for the poor and endless procedural advantages for the wealthy and well-connected.

And the judiciary itself is selected through political appointment or popular election — mechanisms designed to produce politicians in robes, not impartial adjudicators.

Tell me: where, in any of this, is the justice we were promised?

III. The Private Alternative

Now let me describe what a private system of law and justice actually looks like — not in some abstract theoretical vacuum, but building on institutions that already work.

Private Security and Protection:

Imagine competing protection agencies — call them what you like — that offer service contracts to individuals, families, businesses, and communities. They compete on response time, clearance rates, professionalism, and cost. They carry insurance and are bonded. If an agent violates your rights, the company faces direct financial liability — not a taxpayer-funded settlement, but a market consequence that threatens their survival.

These agencies cannot hide behind sovereign immunity. They cannot seize your property without due process. They cannot lobby to maintain their monopoly. They survive only by serving you better than their competitors.

This isn't speculation. Private security personnel in the United States already outnumber sworn police officers roughly three to one. Companies like Securitas, Allied Universal, and thousands of smaller firms protect hospitals, universities, shopping centers, and residential communities — often with lower rates of complaint and misconduct than public police forces.

The question is not whether private security can work. The question is why we artificially cap its potential by preserving a government monopoly over the most critical functions.

Private Courts and Arbitration:

Now, the courts. This is where people grow most nervous, so let me be especially clear.

Private arbitration already resolves the majority of commercial disputes in the world. Organizations like the American Arbitration Association, JAMS, and the International Chamber of Commerce's arbitral body handle complex, high-stakes cases — contract disputes, intellectual property conflicts, even international treaty disagreements — with a fraction of the time and cost of government courts.

In a fully private system, competing arbitration firms would offer their services to resolve disputes — including criminal matters. Individuals and protection agencies would agree, through their contracts, to submit disputes to mutually acceptable arbitrators. These arbitrators would build reputations based on fairness, consistency, and wisdom — because an arbitrator perceived as biased would lose clients from the disadvantaged side and eventually go bankrupt.

This is fundamentally different from government judges, who face no market consequences for incompetence, bias, or cruelty.

"But what about criminal law?" you ask. "What about violence?"

Protection agencies would have contractual obligations to apprehend those who violate the rights of their clients. Disputes between agencies — say, when one agency's client accuses another's — would be resolved through pre-agreed arbitration, just as conflicts between insurance companies are resolved today. The incentive structure favors peaceful resolution, because violent conflict between agencies is expensive — far more expensive than arbitration.

Economist David Friedman has modeled these dynamics extensively. Legal scholar Bruce Benson has documented how private law enforcement historically preceded and outperformed public law enforcement. Edward Stringham's research shows how private governance institutions emerge spontaneously to solve precisely these coordination problems.

IV. Answering the Hard Questions

I know the objections. I respect them. Let me address them directly.

"What about the poor? Won't this be justice only for those who can afford it?"

I ask you: what is the current system if not justice rationed by wealth? The rich hire elite attorneys, post bail effortlessly, and exploit procedural complexity. The poor get overworked public defenders, cash bail they cannot meet, and plea bargains coerced by the threat of disproportionate sentences.

In a competitive market, prices fall and quality rises. We've seen this in every deregulated industry — telecommunications, air travel, computing. Furthermore, charitable legal organizations, mutual aid societies, and community protection cooperatives would fill gaps, just as they did historically before the state monopolized justice. Churches, fraternal organizations, and labor unions once provided extensive mutual protection and dispute resolution for their members.

The poor are not best served by a monopoly that ignores them. They are best served by competition that must earn their trust.

"What prevents protection agencies from becoming warlords?"

Consider the economics. War is the most expensive activity a firm can undertake. Every bullet fired, every agent injured, every property damaged is a cost with no revenue. Agencies that resort to violence against other agencies will see their insurance premiums skyrocket, their customers flee, and their competitors — who resolve disputes peacefully and cheaply — will absorb their market share.

Contrast this with government police and military, which face no competitive pressure, fund themselves through compulsory taxation, and have engaged in more violence, more consistently, than any private actor in human history.

The warlord objection is not an argument against privatization. It is a description of what we already have — and a reason to dismantle it.

"Won't this lead to fragmentation and inconsistency in law?"

To some degree, yes. And that is a feature, not a bug. One-size-fits-all law imposed by a central authority ignores the immense diversity of communities, values, and circumstances across a society. A polycentric legal order allows communities to choose the legal frameworks that best reflect their needs and principles — while market pressure and the demands of inter-community commerce push toward harmonization of core norms, just as the Law Merchant harmonized commercial rules across medieval Europe without any government mandate.

V. The Moral Argument

But beyond the practical case — the better incentives, the greater accountability, the lower costs, the faster resolution — there is a moral argument that I believe is unanswerable.

No one has the right to monopolize justice.

The government claims the exclusive authority to define law, enforce law, and adjudicate law. It claims the right to tax you to fund these services whether you consent or not, whether it performs well or not, whether it respects your rights or not. And if you refuse to pay, if you seek alternatives, if you opt out — it will cage you.

This is not a social contract. You never signed a contract. This is monopoly maintained by force and justified by tradition, inertia, and fear.

Every human being has the right to seek protection. Every human being has the right to seek justice. And every human being has the right to choose who provides it. These rights do not belong to the state. They belong to you.

VI. The Path Forward

I am not naive. I do not expect this transformation overnight. But I urge you to support concrete steps:

First, end qualified immunity. Force government officers to face the same legal liability as every private citizen and security professional. Let the market see how government policing performs when it cannot hide behind legal privilege.

Second, expand the legal scope of private arbitration. Allow individuals to opt into private courts for an ever-wider range of disputes, including criminal matters between consenting parties.

Third, end the legal restrictions and licensing barriers that artificially limit private security. Let communities choose their own protectors.

Fourth, allow tax credits or opt-outs for individuals and communities that provide for their own security and justice. Stop forcing people to pay for a service they do not use and do not want.

Fifth, support legal and constitutional scholarship on polycentric law. Fund research. Host debates. Bring these ideas into the mainstream, where they belong.

VII. Closing

Two hundred and fifty years ago, the idea that government should not control religion was radical. A hundred and fifty years ago, the idea that government should not control speech was still contested. Seventy-five years ago, the idea that government should not control the economy was dismissed as dangerous fantasy.

Today, I am telling you that government should not control justice. And I know how that sounds. I know it feels radical. I know it feels frightening.

But ask yourself: are you satisfied? Are you satisfied with the response times? With the clearance rates? With the plea bargains? With the settlements paid in your name for abuses you never sanctioned? With a system that promises equal justice and delivers anything but?

If you are not satisfied — and I believe you are not — then you owe it to yourself, to your community, and to every person failed by this broken monopoly to consider the alternative.

The alternative is competition. The alternative is accountability. The alternative is choice. The alternative is a system where justice is not a privilege granted by the powerful, but a service earned by those worthy of your trust.

Free the law. Free justice. Free yourselves.

Thank you.

This essay argues persuasively that privatization is not merely preferable but essential, with a particular emphasis on the transformative potential of private security and arbitration over their state-run counterparts.

The superiority of private enterprise begins with its inherent efficiency and cost-effectiveness, qualities that government monopolies can never replicate. The Inherent Inefficiencies of State Monopolies

Government-run services, including police and courts, suffer from the fundamental flaws of monopoly power: lack of competition, bureaucratic inertia, and misaligned incentives. Under government control, police and courts answer to political masters, leading to biases, corruption, and selective enforcement. Judges are either political appointees or politicians themselves, running for election and making decisions with an eye toward public opinion and institutional power.

Private arbitration and private courts solve these defects.

Private dispute resolution is already the dominant form of justice for the most important part of the economy. Almost every commercial contract, every credit card agreement, every employment contract, every international trade deal specifies private arbitration instead of public courts. Why? Because it is faster, cheaper, more expert, and more fair.

In a privatized system, courts would compete on reputation for impartiality and competence. A corrupt or biased arbitration firm would quickly lose business, as no one would agree to include it in their contracts. State courts have no such market discipline. Their customers are captives.

Moreover, a market for law allows the law itself to evolve. In a state system, law is legislation: one-size-fits-all rules imposed from above. In a private system, law is polycentric - a body of precedent built from voluntarily accepted contracts and customary practice. Different communities could choose different legal codes that reflect their values, as long as they respect property rights and non-aggression, rather than being forced into a single Winner-Takes-All legal code imposed by 51% on the other 49%.

3. The Economic and Moral Superiority of Privatization

The economic argument is straightforward: monopoly always costs more and delivers less.

When services are funded through taxation, there is no price signal and no feedback loop. An agency that does a poor job lobbies for a larger budget by claiming its failure proves it needs more resources. An agency that does a good job is rewarded with budget cuts because it appears to need less. This is the recipe for perpetual failure.

Private providers must control costs. They adopt new technology faster. They innovate. Public policing still largely uses mid-20th century models of patrol. Private security firms use real-time GPS tracking, data analytics, drones, and integrated alarm systems because their clients demand value.

There is also a moral argument. All essential services under government control are funded by coercion - taxation under threat of imprisonment. A civilized society should not fund its most important institutions through force. Privatization converts the relationship from coercion to voluntary exchange. You pay for the protection you want, from the provider you trust, and you can withdraw your consent without having to leave the country.

The fear that privatization would mean "justice for only the rich" gets reality backward. Today, justice is already for the rich under state monopoly, because only the rich can afford to navigate the labyrinth of public courts and hire expensive lawyers to deal with overcriminalization. In a competitive market, costs plummet. Just as private cell phones, once a luxury for the rich, are now ubiquitous and cheap, private protection and private arbitration would become affordable for ordinary citizens through insurance models, subscriptions, and homeowners' associations. A neighborhood watch that collectively hires a security firm is far more affordable than bearing the cost of police misconduct lawsuits funded by taxpayers.

4. What Full Privatization Would Look Like

It would not be chaos; it would be order provided by contract.

Roads and infrastructure would be owned by communities and businesses that depend on them, and thus maintained better. Fire protection - which was private for most of American history and still is in many rural areas - would be provided by subscription, as it is in many Arizona and Tennessee counties with excellent results. Defense would be provided by insurance-backed protection agencies and voluntary defense associations, making aggressive war nearly impossible because wars would have to be funded voluntarily instead of through printed money and taxation.

We do not need to guess if this works. We have historical and modern proof: the merchant courts of medieval Europe, the Anglo-Saxon law of restitution before the Norman conquest, modern arbitration in London and Dubai, the private communities of Houston which provide all city services without a municipal government, and the private cities of Prospera, Honduras.

The state does not create order. It parasitizes the order that individuals create through cooperation. For centuries we were told we needed a state monopoly on bread to prevent famine. We were told we needed a state monopoly on religion to prevent moral collapse. Both were false. We are now told we need a state monopoly on security and justice to prevent chaos.

It is time to recognize that superiority of market provision does not stop where government begins. Private security is more effective, more accountable, and more humane than state police. Private arbitration is faster, fairer, and more just than state courts. Complete privatization of essential services is not a leap into the unknown - it is the final step toward a society based on voluntary cooperation instead of coercion.

This is the model advocated by anarcho-capitalists and free-market libertarians - most prominently Murray Rothbard, David Friedman, Bruce Benson, and Hans-Hermann Hoppe. Their arguments for fully privatizing law enforcement and courts are based on economics, accountability, and philosophy:

1. Core Philosophical Reason

Proponents argue that security and dispute resolution are services like any other, and should not be a territorial monopoly. Their premise is:

  • A state monopoly on force cannot be checked by market forces
  • Justice should be based on voluntary contract and restitution to victims, not on a state-defined social contract
  • People should be able to choose and fund only the services and legal norms they consent to

2. Supposed Benefits for Law Enforcement - Private Security Agencies Replacing Public Police

A. Competition and accountability: If a police department provides poor service, citizens cannot easily fire it. If a private security firm provides poor service, clients can cancel their contract and hire a competitor. Proponents argue this creates a direct financial incentive for good behavior. Misconduct would lead to loss of customers, lawsuits, and higher insurance premiums, rather than being protected by qualified immunity and internal review.

B. Economic efficiency: Public police have a guaranteed budget from taxes regardless of performance. Private firms would have to compete on price and quality, which proponents say would lower costs, reduce administrative bloat, and allocate resources based on actual demand for safety.

C. Client-focused service: Public police are said to prioritize enforcement of state priorities - e.g. drug laws, traffic revenue, political order. A private agency paid directly by residents or businesses would be contractually bound to prioritize the client's priorities - protection of life and property, prevention, rapid response.

D. Innovation and specialization: Like other industries, competition would drive innovation - better training, better tech, de-escalation methods, different models for different communities. One neighborhood might want a heavily armed patrol, another might want unarmed community mediators.

E. De-politicization: Police would no longer be an arm of the state that can be used for political purposes, as funding would not come from and control would not rest with politicians.

F. Prevention over enforcement: The model often proposed is insurance-based. Your home/business insurer bundles security. Insurers profit when crime does NOT happen, so they are incentivized to invest in prevention, deterrence, and environmental design, not just arrest after the fact.

3. Supposed Benefits for Judicial Functions - Private Arbitration Replacing State Courts

A. Speed and efficiency: Proponents point to current court backlogs that take months or years. Private arbitration firms, competing for business, would have to offer speedy resolutions or lose clients to faster competitors.

B. Specialization: Instead of a generalist state judge, parties could choose an arbitrator with expertise in the relevant field - commercial contracts, property disputes, family law, tech issues - leading to more informed decisions.

C. Neutrality and choice: In the model, both parties must agree on the arbitrator or arbitration agency in advance by contract. This means neither party gets a home-court advantage. If an arbitration firm develops a reputation for bias, corruption, or bad reasoning, no one will agree to use it.

D. Lower cost: Proponents argue competition would lower legal costs dramatically compared to state courts, which require extensive legal representation and procedure.

E. Focus on restitution vs. punishment: Most models propose a shift from punishment by the state to restitution to the victim. The goal of a ruling would be to make the victim whole, decided by pre-agreed legal principles, rather than incarceration paid for by taxpayers.

4. Systemic Argument - How The System Holds Together

The theory is that private police and private courts would be linked by contract and insurance.

If Person A claims Person B harmed them, A's security agency would not go to war with B's agency. War is expensive. Instead, their contracts would require them to submit the dispute to a mutually agreed-upon third-party arbitrator.

If a person or firm refuses to accept arbitration or refuses to abide by a ruling, they would be blacklisted - their insurance would be canceled, other agencies would refuse to contract with them, businesses would refuse to serve them. In a highly interconnected market, ostracism and economic boycott would replace state coercion.

Proponents cite historical and modern examples they say show pieces of this working: private arbitration already handles most commercial disputes in the US, private security guards already outnumber public police, and systems like medieval Icelandic law and merchant law in Europe operated without a centralized state court.
